scenes.title: A row fixes the first coordinate.
A column fixes the second coordinate.
The second coordinate fixes the column.

cues.text: Chapter Four keeps the floating-point values on the GPU and arranges them in a five by five tensor. Row and column numbers start at zero.
The first coordinate selects a row; the second selects a column. These logical coordinates identify inputs. PyTorch chooses execution details for the CUDA operation.
Read x, zero, colon. Row zero is fixed, while the colon includes all columns. Trace the five highlighted inputs from left to right.
Selecting the row chooses the inputs. Multiplying each selected value by two is a separate calculation, which we will inspect next.
Each output is twice its selected input. The source coordinates beside the values show where every input came from in the original tensor.
This multiplication creates a new result tensor. It leaves the original x unchanged. Selecting a row and calculating its outputs are different parts of the expression.
Now read x, colon, zero. The column is fixed, while the colon includes all rows. We take one input from each row.
The first row and first column share their first value, but the other inputs differ. Both selections still contain five values.
Multiply each column input by two. Each result uses one highlighted input; we are not adding the five values into a single total.
This is elementwise multiplication: apply the operation separately to each selected value. Changing from a row to a column changes the inputs, while the multiplier stays fixed.
With index one, a row selection chooses the second row. A column selection chooses the second column. Compare their five inputs in the diagram.
Keep the multiplier fixed and explain which coordinates changed. A different selection can change the values without changing the number of inputs or the calculation applied to each.
Try x, colon, three, then multiply by two. Before checking, identify which dimension is fixed and which dimension the colon includes.
Trace the five input cells, then predict their five outputs. Does index three mean the fourth row or the fourth column here? Pause and explain.
Index three fixes the fourth column because counting starts at zero. The colon includes every row. The diagram follows those five inputs into their doubled results.
The original tensor is unchanged. Return to Chapter Four, change only a row or column index, and explain the selected inputs before pressing Run.
